questions.question: In Solidity ABI encoding, how are dynamic arguments (like bytes or uint256[]) represented in the head (first 32-byte words)?
options: As 32-byte offsets pointing to their data in the tail
As the raw bytes placed directly in the head
As a keccak256 hash of the argument value
As a 1-byte length followed by the raw bytes
questions.explanation: Dynamic types put an offset in the head; the actual length+data lives in the tail.

questions.question: When a real project ships a broken on-chain verifier integration, which category is more often the root cause?
options: ABI / input-shaping mistakes around the verifier boundary
A fundamental flaw in the pairing-based verifier math
An RNG failure during proof verification on-chain
A Solidity compiler bug that flips the verifier result
questions.explanation: Most incidents are caused by glue code: calldata layout, public input validation, upgrades, or domain separation.

questions.question: You ABI-encode arguments for (bytes proof, uint256[] pubSignals) with no function selector. The head is 64 bytes. If proof is 33 bytes, what offset (in bytes) should pubSignals start at in strict encoding?
questions.explanation: The proof tail is 32 (length word) + ceil32(33)=64 bytes, total 96. So offset is 64 + 96 = 160.

questions.question: Why do many verifier wrappers enforce pubSignals[i] < SNARK_SCALAR_FIELD before calling the autogenerated verifier?
options: Because uint256 arithmetic would overflow otherwise
Because EVM curve/scalar operations may implicitly reduce modulo the field/order, allowing multiple byte encodings for the same field element
Because the verifier contract cannot read calldata without the check
Because Solidity requires all uint256 values to be prime
questions.explanation: Circuits work over a finite field. If the on-chain path implicitly reduces values modulo that field/order, out-of-range inputs can become alternate encodings of the same element.

questions.question: After EIP-2028-style pricing, which calldata is cheaper (all else equal)?
options: A payload with mostly 0x00 bytes
A payload with mostly random non-zero bytes
They cost the same per byte
The random payload is cheaper because it compresses better
questions.explanation: Zero bytes are priced lower than non-zero bytes (commonly modeled as 4 vs 16 gas/byte).

questions.question: Which wrapper behavior most directly prevents an attacker from providing a truncated or reshaped public input vector?
options: Enforce pubSignals.length equals the expected count
Convert pubSignals to bytes with abi.encodePacked
Emit an event before verification
Cache pubSignals in storage
questions.explanation: Length checking ensures the verifier is called with exactly the arity the circuit expects.

questions.question: Attack scenario: a project uses a verifier but never checks pubSignals[i] < SNARK_SCALAR_FIELD. Which risk is most realistic?
options: Users can submit out-of-range values that reduce modulo the field/order, creating multiple representations and breaking application-level bindings (e.g., nullifier uniqueness)
The blockchain will halt because the verifier enters an infinite loop
The prover can recover the verification key from the contract storage
The verifier becomes constant-time automatically, so side channels disappear
questions.explanation: Without range checks, the same field element can have multiple uint256 encodings if reduction occurs, which can invalidate assumptions like uniqueness or exact byte-level commitments.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of generating a defensive Solidity wrapper around an autogenerated verifier contract?
options: Re-implement the pairing checks in Solidity for transparency
Enforce application invariants (lengths, ranges, governance constraints) before delegating to the verifier
Make proofs zero-knowledge on-chain by encrypting calldata
Remove the need for test vectors
questions.explanation: Wrappers handle app-specific checks and lifecycle concerns; the autogenerated verifier remains the cryptographic core.
